One-Owner 1963 Plymouth Fury Ragtop Sat 20 Years in a Barn, 140k-Mile Poly V8 Can Still Do a Burnout
64 photos
Photo: YouTube/Rocket Restorations
1963 was how long ago? SIXTY-THREE years? Already?!?! Boy, and here I was, looking at brass-era cars and thinking “So, that’s how cars looked like 50 years ago.” Time has a bad habit of speeding up as it gets closer to the finish line, doesn’t it? Well, this one-owner Plymouth Fury could beg to differ – its past decades haven’t been exactly in a hurry to get it anywhere. Now it finally got a well-deserved, long-awaited resurrection.
Introduced for 1956 as a high-performance sub-series of the Belvedere, the Plymouth Fury became a standalone model line from 1959 through 1978 across seven distinct generations. The moniker rode on full-size body-on-frame chassis through 1959, full-size unibodies from 1960 to 1961, intermediate B-body platforms from 1962 to 1964 and 1975 to 1978, and full-size C-body architecture from 1965 to 1974, peaking in 1969 when fuselage C-body production approached 367,000 units.
Restyled on a 116-inch B-body wheelbase for 1963, midsize Plymouth production reached 244,395 cars, split between 158,612 V8s and 85,783 six-cylinders, though Chrysler kept no transmission totals by trim. The Fury series accounted for 67,584 vehicles, comprising 31,891 four-door sedans and 13,832 two-door hardtops in six-cylinder and V8 forms, plus 11,877 four-door hardtops, 5,221 convertibles, 2,352 six-passenger wagons, and 2,411 nine-passenger wagons with V8 power, alongside 15,319 V8 Sport Furys.
Buyers in 1963 paired a standard 3-speed column-shift manual, an optional pushbutton 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic, or a mid-year 4-speed manual with a 145-hp 225 Slant-Six, a 230-hp Polyspherical 318 V8, a 265-hp 361-cubic-inch V8, a 330-hp 383 V8, or the 415-hp/425-hp 426-cubic-inch Max Wedge V8.
Photo: YouTube/Rocket Restorations Base pricing spanned from $2,563 for the six-cylinder Fury four-door sedan to $3,071 for the nine-passenger wagon and $3,082 for the Sport Fury convertible. Standard V8 Fury convertibles carried a $2,924 base price, including one example scheduled for assembly in Detroit, Michigan, on December 24, 1962, and shipped to Chrysler City, Inc. in Portland, Oregon. This red relic who ended up with the short stick, and was relegated to bird toilet duties for way too long.
Optioned with a $162.10 Basic Radio Group, a $49.75 Sure Grip differential, $47.58 for 7.50x14 whitewall tires, a $21.55 tinted windshield, an $11.80 dual-jet washer, $5.60 for antifreeze, and a $157 destination charge, its factory window sticker reached $3,379.38. In 1963, that was quite the investment. Consider this: that year, the same amount would buy you a 409-Impala. The dual-quad, 400-hp version.
Because this red drop-top paired its 230-hp 318-cubic-inch Polyspherical V8 with a column-shifted 3-speed manual transmission , manual steering, and manual drum brakes, showroom shoppers ignored it for eight months. On August 22, 1963, Pacific Trailways bus driver Donald H. Richardson offered cash with no trade-in, securing a $667.18 discount to buy the convertible for $2,712.20 plus $12 in license and title fees. That’s what I call a deal – 20% off in the blink of an eye.
Photo: YouTube/Rocket Restorations Richardson immediately put the Plymouth to work, affixing a Dymo label with his name and employer to the inside mirror and paying $15.44 for three Safety King seat belts. Invoices preserved in his original folder chronicle a trailer hitch and tachometer installation at Armory Automotive Service in Portland at 654 miles, a clutch adjustment at Dalton Motors in Sacramento, California, at 1,430 miles, and replacement rear quarter trim in 1965.
In 1972, Richardson moved the convertible to a farm, a mile outside Pomeroy, Washington, where the dry climate protected its floor pans, rocker panels, and convertible torque boxes. Over the following decades, he installed dual exhaust tailpipes for $25.08 in 1984, rebuilt the front suspension in 1988, paid $333 for a black top in January 1989, and had Motor Works, Inc. overhaul the engine at 109,851 miles in February 1993.
Richardson drove the Fury another 30,733 miles to reach 140,584 total miles, fitting a bumper flag bracket for parades and registering Washington Collector Vehicle plates in October 2010 before passing away in 2022 after 59 years of ownership. After the car sat idle for nearly four years, Tom Hergert, front man and head wrencher of the Rocket Restorations YouTube channel, bought it from Richardson's daughter Sheila and sent his brother, Gary Hergert, to retrieve it.
Photo: YouTube/Rocket Restorations Following a five-hour drive (each way) to Pomeroy, Gary winched the Plymouth from an open farm shed where birds roosting on an overhead beam had buried the lowered top and red vinyl split-bench interior under thick droppings. Joined at the shop by assistant Evan and chief mechanic Jamie Attwood (himself host of his own Dead Dodge Garage YouTube channel), Tom vacuumed mouse carcasses from the cabin and scrubbed the driver's seat clean.
Taking charge of the mechanical revival, Jamie Attwood topped off the brake master cylinder and pumped the brake pedal enough times to call it a leg day workout, until hydraulic pressure returned. After connecting a fresh battery and watching the dashboard ammeter dip to confirm ignition continuity, he sampled the fuel tank behind the rear license plate, replaced a cracked rubber fuel hose, added half a gallon of coolant, and primed the two-barrel Stromberg carburetor with gasoline.
On the first turn of the key, the 318-cubic-inch V8 fired immediately and idled smoothly on old gasoline while the headlights, windshield wipers, and Conelrad AM radio came back to life. Hergert drove the Fury onto the grass to wash off decades of filth before a sudden rainstorm forced the crew to lift the power top manually, after which he unbolted two homemade trunk plates hiding huge rodent nests.
Photo: YouTube/Rocket Restorations After vacuuming the trunk troughs, pulling the lower quarter panel drain plugs on the shop lift, flushing the cavities with water, and soaking them in Lysol, the team tackled the mechanical leaks. While Evan wired a replacement passenger-side taillight socket, Hergert cured a severe engine oil leak by replacing a pinched oil filter adapter gasket and messy silicone sealant, spinning on a shorter Wix filter with fresh high-zinc oil.
To silence a noisy front end, Attwood removed the radiator and four-blade fan, transferred the heater hose thread adapter bushing into a new cast-iron MasterPro water pump, and installed a single-pulley alternator, fresh hoses, and a new V-belt. After testing the Sure Grip axle with smoky burnouts, Attwood test-drove the Fury at 50 mph on its first outing in 20 years before Tom Hergert takes the car back to the original owner’s wife, Sheila, to showcase the resurrected Mopar.
Having one owner its entire existence was a definitive plus for the classic, and having own that cared for it is probably why we got to see it brought back to life (play the two videos below for two original versions of the same revival) in such an expeditious manner. There are some minor details to address, such as the power top, or fresh tires, but the key elements are done for. If only all barn finds resurrections were this good…
